newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY LEAGUE-BULLS KICK HOLE IN SUPER LEAGUE IMAGE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY LEAGUE-BULLS KICK HOLE IN SUPER LEAGUE IMAGE.

text.p: Super League plans to change the rules of its World Club Challenge next season after England's Bradford Bulls qualified for the quarter-finals without winning a match.

Bradford turned sporting logic on its head last weekend by reaching the last eight in the competition involving Euro League and Australian Super League clubs despite losing all six matches in the qualifying round.
They owed their passage to a format that favours European clubs by guaranteeing them four berths in the quarter-finals whatever their results against Australian opponents.
As a result of that system, Sydney-based club Penrith missed out despite winning all their six matches against English teams, including a 54-14 drubbing of the Bulls.
"The outcome certainly has not helped Super League's credibility," a spokeswoman for the competition said.
She said Super League planned to change the rules and composition of the World Club Challenge next season, limiting entry to the top four teams in each league.
Bradford will play Auckland Warriors in the quarter-finals, to be played on the weekend of October 4-5.
Penrith were edged out in their qualifying group on points difference behind Brisbane, Auckland and Cronulla, who all won their six games.
By contrast, the six teams in the Euro League's top pool, including traditional powers Wigan and St Helens, had only three victories between them.
Bradford finished third in the group, edging out St Helens for a certain place by losing their games by smaller margins.
Australian clubs won most of their matches with embarrassing ease, regularly racking up 50 points or more against some poor English defences.
"The scorelines have been embarrassing at times," the spokeswoman said. "We were surprised that the competition has been so one-sided.
"We decided on the format because we wanted the Euro League teams to have as much opportunity as possible to qualify for the quarter-finals.
"We definitely tried to favour the English teams, knowing that they were not as good," she added.
The competition had the benefit of alerting the English rugby league ruling body to the massive gap in playing standards between the two countries at club level, she added.
